\paragraph{Model Collapse in Recursive Training.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024} provided the first systematic empirical study of model collapse, showing that iteratively training on self-generated data leads to progressive loss of distributional tails.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{strong_collapse2025} formalized this theoretically, proving that collapse occurs even under optimal retraining conditions.
Subsequent work characterized collapse through an information-theoretic lens~\cite{entropy_collapse2025}, demonstrating monotonic entropy decrease across generations.
A critical gap remains: these analyses are post-hoc diagnostics, offering no mechanism for \emph{online} detection or intervention during training.

\paragraph{Spectral Monitoring of Representations.}
Building on the need for online signals, Garrido et al.~\cite{rankme2023} introduced RankMe, showing that the effective rank of representation matrices correlates strongly with downstream performance without requiring labeled evaluation.
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} extended spectral analysis to monitor training dynamics, identifying phase transitions in learned representations.
These works establish spectral health as a reliable, low-cost proxy for representation quality, yet neither closes the loop by using spectral signals to \emph{drive} corrective action.

\paragraph{Static Data Mixing Strategies.}
One natural corrective is mixing real data into synthetic training.
He et al.~\cite{he2025golden} proposed a fixed ``golden ratio'' for synthetic-to-real mixing that minimizes degradation under i.i.d.\ assumptions.
Garg et al.~\cite{garg2025} provided theoretical bounds on optimal proportions as a function of distribution shift, and further empirical work~\cite{mixing2026} validated that even small real-data fractions substantially slow collapse.
However, all these approaches prescribe a \emph{static} ratio, ignoring temporal dynamics: early generations need less real data while later generations facing accelerating collapse require more.

\paragraph{Data Accumulation and Adaptive Selection.}
Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024} showed that accumulating all past data avoids collapse, but the approach is inapplicable under fixed budget constraints.
Recursive stability theory~\cite{recursive_stability2025} proves that a constant real-data proportion ensures convergence, motivating adaptive optimization of that proportion rather than fixing it a priori.
Among adaptive methods, DCES~\cite{dces2026} rebalances sampling \emph{within} the synthetic pool via intra-cluster dispersion, and ADAPT~\cite{adapt2025} learns task-level proportions under explicit token budgets for multi-task tuning.
Neither adapts the global real/synthetic ratio, nor uses spectral health as the control signal.

\paragraph{Calibration and Knowledge Preservation.}
Complementary work has monitored calibration drift~\cite{calibration2025} and knowledge collapse~\cite{knowledge_collapse2025} as degradation signals orthogonal to spectral indicators.
Whether spectral or calibration metrics provide earlier warning remains an open empirical question.
Our work is the first to close the loop: using a spectral early-warning signal to drive \emph{budget-constrained temporal allocation} of real data across recursive training generations.

Training language models on their own synthetic outputs across multiple generations leads to \emph{model collapse}, a progressive narrowing of the learned distribution that degrades generation quality~\cite{shumailov2024}.
Recent empirical and theoretical work reveals that this degradation is not linear: spectral contraction in representation spaces accelerates around generation 20~\cite{sigma2026}, tail distributions compound with each generation~\cite{shumailov2024}, and degradation rates double past inflection points in the synthetic proportion~\cite{calibration2025}.
This non-linear acceleration makes the \emph{timing} of corrective intervention as important as its magnitude.

The dominant mitigation strategy is mixing real data into the synthetic training pipeline.
Theoretical analyses identify optimal static mixing ratios, notably the golden ratio $\phi^{-1} \approx 0.618$~\cite{he2025golden}, and data accumulation strategies that prevent collapse in principle~\cite{gerstgrasser2024, garg2025}.
However, static ratios assume constant collapse pressure across generations, an assumption contradicted by the empirical evidence of non-linear acceleration.
Meanwhile, spectral monitoring tools like SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} diagnose collapse in rich detail but prescribe no intervention.
Adaptive sampling methods such as DCES~\cite{dces2026} redistribute \emph{within} the synthetic pool but do not control the global real-to-synthetic ratio.
No existing system closes the feedback loop from spectral diagnosis to adaptive real-data allocation.

We present, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop system connecting spectral collapse monitoring to budget-constrained adaptive mixing.
Our key insight is that a fixed real-data budget achieves improved collapse prevention when allocated \emph{temporally}, with real data concentrated at generations of peak collapse pressure rather than spread uniformly.
We monitor representational health via effective rank~\cite{rankme2023} and spectral log-volume of output embeddings, and feed the spectral log-volume signal into a proportional controller that adjusts the real-data fraction generation-by-generation while guaranteeing total budget adherence.
